label: hood missing filter
description:
A commercial kitchen exhaust hood that is missing one or more whole baffle-filter panels from its filter rack—including a rack from which every filter has been removed—leaving the plenum exposed through the filter plane.
Identify the filter rack first: the mounting track or framed rack with top and bottom retaining rails where slatted metal baffle filters are designed to seat. The rack may be fully populated, partially empty, or completely empty.
Apply this label when one or more full panel positions in the rack are empty, exposing the plenum behind. This INCLUDES a bank where all filters have been removed—if you can see the empty rack or its mounting rails running along where filters should be, with no filters installed, apply the label.
Do NOT apply for:
- A hood with no baffle-filter rack at all—a plain canopy, a bare exhaust duct, or a hood not designed to hold baffle filters. Do not read open or greasy canopy space as an empty rack; there must be a recognizable filter rack or mounting track where panels belong.
- The dark canopy end, corner, or plenum area beyond where the filter rack stops—that is not a filter slot.
- A slot filled with aluminum foil, a solid blanking panel, cardboard, or other material—that slot is filled, not missing.
- A slanted, dislodged, or damaged filter, or a gap beside an installed filter (those are bypass gaps).
In the classification explanation, state whether some or all panel positions are empty and identify the rack or retaining-rail evidence.

label: hood grease buildup
description:
Visible grease deposit on an interior surface of a commercial kitchen exhaust hood: panels, filters, visible baffle-channel interiors, or filter rails/troughs.
First confirm that the affected surface belongs to the hood interior. Exterior canopy faces, nearby walls, backsplashes, and cooking equipment do not qualify. Inspect each visible area, especially channel recesses, lower filter edges, seams, and the rails above and below the filters.
Thick or caked buildup is NOT required. Apply this label when any eligible interior area shows a deposited grease feature, including:
- A tacky, filmy, or textured grease coating forming irregular patches, streaks, or layering across a filter face, channel, or multiple baffles.
- Yellow, orange, or brown grease discoloration or staining of the interior metal (as distinct from plain gray metal aging).
- Grease dripping, hanging in droplets, leaving residue-bearing drip trails, or pooling—including drips along or below the filter rails/track.
- Raised, crusted, lumpy, burnt-looking, or caked grease.
A clean-looking surrounding surface does not negate a qualifying deposit. Deposits may be thin as long as they are clearly grease rather than a reflection.
Exclude: a thin, uniform light grease film consistent with normal operational use; scattered fine specks without a coating; reflections, shadows, soot alone, corrosion, water/condensation, cleaning marks, adhesive/sticker residue, and pipe fittings/sealant; a grease collection cup or trough catching grease as designed; and minor metal discoloration from age rather than grease.
Do not apply this label if no qualifying deposit is visible or its interior location cannot be established. Do not infer hidden buildup.
In the classification explanation, identify the affected component, its location, and the specific deposit feature (color, texture, drip) supporting the label.

label: hood bypass gap
description:
A filter bypass gap: an unintended opening or separation that lets air bypass the filter media, caused by a panel that is misaligned, unseated, tilted, mismatched, damaged, or not flush with its neighbors or the frame—or by a damaged baffle channel within a panel.
Do NOT default to "properly seated," and do NOT judge by size. A bypass gap can be larger than, the same size as, or smaller than a normal baffle channel—even a separation of an inch or less between two panels is a valid gap. Inspect closely:
- Between two adjacent panels: any visible separation, step, or dark line where they do not sit flush—any width, even very narrow.
- At a panel's top or bottom edge against the frame rail: any opening where it is not seated tight.
- At the end of the bank: a gap between the last panel and the hood's side wall or frame.
- A damaged baffle channel: a baffle that is bent, torn, crushed, broken, or deformed, creating an opening through to the plenum. This qualifies even when the opening is the same size as an intact channel.
- A tilted, bowed, recessed, protruding, or dislodged panel creating an opening at a corner or edge.
Apply this label when any such opening, separation, or damaged channel is visible, even if small.
To distinguish a real gap from a filter's own design: an intact, properly seated panel has evenly spaced, uniform, undamaged vertical baffle channels—those are NOT gaps. A gap is an opening between panels, at an edge or frame, or where a channel is damaged, irregular, or broken.
Do NOT apply for: the uniform, undamaged internal channels of a properly seated panel; reflections, highlights, or dark bands on the filter face; or handles, frame rails, and grease staining by themselves. An entirely empty slot is a missing filter, not a bypass gap.
In the classification explanation, name which panel, edge, or damaged channel the opening is at.
